summary: Mars: Outpost Zero is a browser-based exploration and survival game that teaches real facts about Mars through play. Players take the role of a Commander on a Martian base, helped by a small robot called BIP. They complete ten missions, such as cleaning dust off solar panels, surviving a solar storm and building an exploration vehicle. They balance energy, supplies and radiation shielding, and unlock new regions. Each mission ends with a discovery linked to its original NASA source. Our own fictional elements are labelled as simulated. The game also has a hoverbike, a compass, a live map, a decorable home with a credit economy, and a Mars Lab with minigames. It runs in one HTML file on desktop and mobile, with no installation. It matters because it makes space science approachable and fun for young learners while staying transparent about what is real and what is invented.
details:
Players explore six connected regions of Mars on foot or by hoverbike along dirt trails, guided by a compass and a live map. Ten missions use different interactions (tapping, timing, pattern memory, trade-off choices) and change energy, supplies and radiation bars, so every choice has a cost. Missions earn credits and unlock regions. Credits buy furniture for the home; each piece has a price, a collision-checked footprint, rotation and a preview. The Mars Lab adds two minigames, Power Grid and Drone Run, with their own mechanics. Each level pays only once, so rewards cannot be farmed. Progress is saved in the browser.

Impact: players learn real facts, such as Mars gravity being about 37% of Earth’s. Each discovery links to its NASA source, and invented elements are labelled as simulated.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript in one file; Canvas 2D for all art, including procedural furniture and trail textures; Web Audio for synthesized sound; localStorage for saves. No external assets. Built with AI assistance, disclosed in the credits.

Creativity: exploration, resource management, decoration and varied minigames in one self-generated world.

Factors considered: honesty about sources, touch and keyboard support, any screen size, light performance, and protection against duplicated purchases and rewards.
